In [[mathematics]], '''vector bundles on algebraic curves''' may be studied as [[holomorphic vector bundle]]s on [[compact Riemann surface]]s, which is the classical approach, or as [[locally free sheaves]] on [[algebraic curve]]s ''C'' in a more general, algebraic setting (which can for example admit [[Mathematical singularity|singular points]]).

Some foundational results on classification were known in the 1950s. The result of {{Harvtxt|Grothendieck|1957}}, that holomorphic vector bundles on the [[Riemann sphere]] are sums of [[line bundle]]s, is now often called the '''[[Birkhoff–Grothendieck theorem]]''', since it is implicit in much earlier work of {{Harvtxt|Birkhoff|1909}} on the [[Riemann–Hilbert problem]].

{{Harvtxt|Atiyah|1957}} gave the classification of vector bundles on [[elliptic curve]]s.

The Riemann–Roch theorem for vector bundles was proved by {{Harvtxt|Weil|1938}}, before the 'vector bundle' concept had really any official status. Although, associated [[ruled surface]]s were classical objects. See [[Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem]] for his result. He was seeking a generalization of the [[Jacobian variety]], by passing from [[holomorphic line bundle]]s to higher rank. This idea would prove fruitful, in terms of [[moduli space]]s of vector bundles. following on the work in the 1960s on [[geometric invariant theory]].
